en: One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha;
for one begins the chant with "Om.
Here follows its further explanation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1)
Of these beings, the earth is the essence;
of the earth, water is the essence;
of water, plants are the essence.
Of herbs, man is the essence;
of man, speech is the essence;
of speech, the Ṛg-veda is the essence.
The Ṛgveda has the Sāman as its essence;
the Sāman has the Udgītha as its essence.
This very Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth.
"What is the Ṛk? What is the Sāman? What is the Udgītha?"—thus it was deliberated upon. ChU 1.1.4.
Speech indeed is the Ṛk; breath is the Sāman;
this syllable "Om" is the Udgītha.
Now, this indeed is a union: speech and breath, and the Ṛk and the Sāman.
This pair is united in this syllable "Om.
Indeed, when a pair comes together, they fulfill each other's desire.
He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha. 1.1.7.
This, indeed, is the syllable of assent. For whatever one assents to, one says "Om" to that.
Assent itself is prosperity.
Verily, he becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.8)
Therefore, this triple knowledge proceeds thus:
with "Oṃ" he causes the announcement; with "Oṃ" he recites the praise.
He sings the Udgītha as "Om," for the sake of honoring this very syllable, through its greatness and its essence.
Therefore, both perform [the sacrifice]:
he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different.
"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful. This indeed is the further explanation of this very syllable.

Once, when the gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another, the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By this we shall overcome them. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.1)
They meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it.
For he is pierced by evil.
Then they indeed worshipped speech as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of that [speech], one speaks both the true and the false.
For she has been pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the eye as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the ear as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one hears both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing.
For this is pierced by evil. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.5)
Then they venerated the mind as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one intends both that which is to be intended and that which is not.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then, they meditated upon that very breath which is the principal one as the Udgītha.
When the Asuras attacked it, they were shattered, just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a solid stone. ChU 1.2.7.

Just as a clod of earth striking a solid stone is shattered, even so is he shattered who desires evil against one who knows this, and he who seeks to harm him; for such a person is like that clod of earth against the stone. 1.2.8.
By this [breath], one perceives neither fragrance nor foul odor,
for it is free from evil.
Whatever it eats and whatever it drinks, by that it sustains the other vital breaths.
Indeed, having failed to find this even at the end, he departs;
for he opens his mouth wide at the very end. Thus it is said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.9)
Aṅgiras meditated upon that as the Udgītha;
for they consider this very one to be Aṅgirasa, since he is the essence of the limbs.
With this, Bṛhaspati indeed meditated upon that Udgītha.
And they consider him to be Bṛhaspati;
for speech is the Great (Bṛhatī), and he is its lord.
Therefore, he meditated upon that Udgītha as Āyāsya;
for they indeed consider this very one to be Āyāsya,
because it proceeds from the mouth (āsya).
By this means, Baka Dālbhya indeed came to know it;
he became the Udgātṛ priest for the residents of Naimiṣa,
and he used to obtain all desires for them by singing.
"Verily, one becomes an attainer of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha.
This is with reference to the self. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.14)
Now, with reference to the deities:
one should meditate upon that very sun which shines as the Udgītha.
Indeed, rising, it sings the Udgītha for the sake of all creatures.
Rising, it dispels the fear of darkness;
indeed, he who knows this becomes a dispeller of the fear of darkness. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.1)
This one here and that one yonder are indeed the same:
this one is warm, and that one is warm.
They call this one "sound" (svara), and they call that one "echo" (pratyāsvara).
Therefore, one should indeed meditate upon this Udgītha as both this [earth] and that [heaven].
Now, one should indeed meditate upon vyāna as the udgītha.
That which one breathes out is prāṇa; that which one breathes in is apāna.
Now, that which is the junction of the out-breath and the in-breath is the diffused breath (vyāna). That which is the diffused breath is speech.
Therefore, one utters speech without breathing out and without breathing in.
Speech is the *ṛc*; therefore, one utters the *ṛc* without breathing in or breathing out. That which is the *ṛc* is the *sāman*.
Therefore, one sings the Sāman without breathing out or breathing in.
That which is the Sāman is the Udgītha;
therefore, one chants the Udgītha without breathing out or breathing in.

Therefore, whatever other vigorous actions there are—such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a stiff bow—he performs them without breathing in or breathing out. For this reason, one should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the *vyāna* breath itself. (ChU 1.3.5)
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*: namely, *ut*, *gī*, and *tha*. *Ut* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for by means of the vital breath one rises up.
*Vāk* is *gīḥ*; for they call speech *giraḥ*. *Anna* is *tham*.
For on food indeed all this is supported. // ChUp 1.3.6 //
Heaven is indeed the *ut*,
the intermediate space is the *gīr*,
and the earth is the *tham*.
Āditya is the *ut*;
Vāyu is the *gīḥ*;
Agni is the *tham*.
The Sāmaveda is indeed the *ut*,
the Yajurveda is the *gīḥ*,
and the Ṛgveda is the *tham*.

Speech yields its milk for him who knows the milking of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food, who, knowing these syllables of the Udgītha thus, meditates upon them as "ud-gī-tha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.7)
Now, indeed, there is the fulfillment of one's prayer.
One should worship with the "approaches" (upasaraṇas). With whatever Sāman one intends to chant, that Sāman one should meditate upon.
One should meditate upon that Ṛṣi who is the seer of the Ṛc in which one is about to praise, and upon that deity whom one is about to praise. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.9)
One should meditate upon that very metre with which one intends to praise;
one should meditate upon that very hymn-form (stoma) with which one is about to praise. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.10)
In whichever direction one intends to praise, toward that direction one should run.
Having approached the Self at the very end, one should praise it while meditating on the desired object with vigilance.

For that desired object for which one praises will quickly be fulfilled—whatever desire one may have when praising, whatever desire one may have when praising. Thus ends the third section of the first chapter.
One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha;
for with "Om" one sings the Udgītha. Here follows its detailed explanation.

The gods, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge. They covered themselves with the meters; because they covered themselves with them, that is the "metrical" nature (*chandastva*) of the meters. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.2)
Thereupon Death beheld them there, just as one might look for a fish in water, within the Ṛg-veda, the Sāman-veda, and the Yajur-veda.
But having discovered them, they rose above the Ṛg, the Sāman, and the Yajus, and entered into the very tone itself.
When one encounters a Ṛg-verse, one utters "Om" as its supreme tone; so too with a Sāman, and so too with a Yajus.
This syllable is indeed that tone; it is immortal and fearless.
Having entered into it, the gods became immortal.
He who, knowing this thus, utters the syllable Om, enters that very syllable—the sound, the immortal, the fearless.
Having entered it, he becomes immortal, even as the gods are immortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.5)
Now, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the Udgītha;
it is the Praṇava, for it moves along uttering "Om."
"It was precisely this that I meditated upon; therefore you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"Turn the reins around;
indeed, many sons shall be yours."
Thus with reference to the deities. ChUp 1.5.2.
Now, with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that which is this chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*.
For it goes forth sounding "Om."
"It was precisely this that I sang; therefore you are my only one," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"Sing to the breaths as the Plurality; then many indeed will be mine. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.4)

Now, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava, and that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. For even from the seat of the Hotṛ priest, one can rectify a poorly performed Udgītha—yes, one can rectify it. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.5)
This very [Ṛgveda] is the Ṛc; Agni is the Sāman.
Thus, this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc. This [earth] is the Sāman; Agni is the Āma.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.6.1.
The intermediate space is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the wind is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The intermediate space itself is the Sāman;
the wind is the Ama.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.6.2.
The sky is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the sun is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superposed upon the Ṛc. The sky is indeed the Sāman;
the sun is the Am.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.6.3.
The stars are the *ṛc* and the moon is the *sāman*; thus,
this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc. The stars are the Sāman;
the moon is the Āma.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.6.4.
Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly dark, is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc.
Now, that which is the white light of this sun is *sā*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is *amaḥ*.
That is *sāman*.
Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with a golden beard and golden hair, is entirely golden down to his very fingernails.
His eyes are like a lotus flower that is as yellow as the buttocks of a monkey;
his name is "Ut" (risen up),
for he has risen up above all evils.
Verily, he who knows this rises up above all evils. ChUp 1.6.7.
The Ṛk and the Sāman are his two singers;
therefore he is the Udgītha,
and for that very reason, he is the Udgātṛ priest.
For he is the singer of this [Sāman].
He is the lord of those worlds that are beyond yonder sun, and of the desires of the gods.
Thus far with respect to the divine. (ChU 1.6.8)
Now, with reference to the self:
speech indeed is the Ṛk,
and breath is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. That [Ṛc] is indeed speech.
The vital breath is *ama*;
that is the *sāman*.
The eye is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the self (*ātman*) is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is established upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The eye is indeed the Sāman; the self is the Ṛc.
That is the Sāman. ChU 1.7.2.
The ear is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the mind is the *sāman*;
thus this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The ear indeed is the Sāman; the mind is the Am.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.7.3.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the dark, the deep black, is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the Sāman;
and that which is the dark, the deep black, is the Āma.
That is Sāman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.4)
Now, that person who is seen within the eye— he is indeed the Ṛg,
he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha.
That is the Yajus;
that is the Brahman.
Of this very one, the form is the same as the form of that [other].
Whatever are his joints, those are its joints;
whatever is its name, that is its name.
He is the one who rules over those worlds that are on this side of him, and over the desires of men.
Therefore, when these people sing to the lute, they sing of him; hence they are winners of wealth.
Now, he who, knowing this thus, sings the Sāman, he sings to both.
By means of that [sun] alone, he obtains those worlds which are beyond it, as well as the desires of the gods.
Moreover, by this very [knowledge], he attains those worlds that are below this one, as well as the desires of human beings.
Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say: [ChU 1.7.8]
"What desire shall I sing forth for you?
For he who, knowing this, sings the Sāman, indeed has mastery over the singing of desires; he who, knowing this, sings the Sāman, sings the Sāman.
There were three men who were experts in the Udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali.
They said, "We are indeed experts in the Udgītha; come, let us have a discussion on the Udgītha."
"So be it," they replied, and sat down together.
Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said,
"Let your honors speak first."
"I shall listen to the words of the two wandering mendicants as they speak. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.2)
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come, let me question you.
"Ask," he replied.
"What is the goal of the Sāman? "The tone," he said. "What is the goal of the tone?"
"Life-breath," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Food," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Water," he said.
"What is the goal of the waters?
"That world," he said.
"What is the goal of that world?"
"It would not lead one to the heavenly world," he said.
"We establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world,
for the Sāman is a hymn of praise to heaven."
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.6)
"Come, let me know this from the Blessed One.
"Know it," he said. "What is the goal of that world?"
"This is the world," he said. "What is the goal of this world? "One should not lead it beyond its foundation," he replied.
"We establish the world as the foundation through the Sāman; for the Sāman is indeed a praise based on the foundation. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.7)
Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him:
"O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite.
If someone were to say now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would fall off."
"Come, let me learn this from the Blessed One.
"Learn it," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.8)
"What is the goal of this world?
"Space," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings arise from space alone."
They pass away into space;
for space is indeed greater than these,
and space is their ultimate resort.
This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high;

this is infinite. For him who, knowing it thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as the higher than the high, there becomes a world higher than the high, and he conquers worlds higher than the high. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2)
Atidhanvan Śaunaka, having taught this very Udgītha to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said:
"As long as they shall know this Udgītha among their offspring, so long will there be a superior life for them in this world."
"Likewise, there will be a world for him in yonder world.

He who, knowing this, meditates upon it, his life in yonder world becomes even higher and more excellent, and likewise there is a world for him in yonder world—yes, a world, a world! Thus ends the first section of the first chapter.
When the Kuru country was devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a beggar in the village of a wealthy man, together with his wife Āṭikī.
He begged from him as he was eating some sour gruel.
He said to him,
"There are no others than these which have been set before me."
"Give these to me," he said.
He gave them to him, saying,
"Behold, here is a drink for you."
"I would indeed have drunk what is left over," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.3)
"Are these not also leftovers?
"No," he said, "I would not have lived without eating them;
for me, water is a matter of desire."
Having eaten, he brought the remainder to his wife;
even before she had finished, she became well-fed.
She took them and set them aside.
As he was rising in the morning, he said:
"If only we could obtain some food! We might obtain a measure of wealth;
this king is going to perform a sacrifice."
"Let him choose me for all the priestly offices," he said.
His wife said to him, "Come now, husband;
here are these very beans.
Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which was being performed.
There he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the Stotra.
He then said to the Prastotṛ: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.8.
"O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.9)
In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ:
"O Udgātṛ, if you perform the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter apart."
In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ priest:
"O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter apart.
Terrified, they remained silent.
Then the sacrificer said to him,
"I desire to know you, O Blessed One.
He replied, "I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa."
He said:
"I have indeed sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly offices;
it was only because I did not know your worth that I chose others."
"But let the Blessed One himself perform all the priestly offices for me.
"So be it," [the Blessed One replied].
"In that case, let these very priests, being fully authorized, offer the praise."
"As long as you would give wealth to these [other priests], so much should you give to me. "So be it," the sacrificer replied.
Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said:
"Sir, you said to me, 'O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off.
Which is that deity? CHU 1.11.4.
"It is *prāṇa*," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings enter into *prāṇa* alone,
and from *prāṇa* they emerge."
This very deity is connected with the Prastāva.
If you had chanted the Prastāva without knowing her, your head would have fallen off, as I have told you.
Then the Udgātṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is associated with the Udgītha, your head will fall off.
Which is that deity? ChU 1.11.6.
"It is Āditya," he said.
"Indeed, all these beings sing to Āditya as he is high above.
This deity is connected with the Udgītha."
"If you had sung that [hymn] without knowing it while facing northward, your head would have fallen off, even though you were told so by me."
Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you said to me, 'O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is associated with the Pratihāra, your head will shatter.
Which is that deity?"
"Food," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings live by taking hold of food alone.
This deity is dependent upon the Pratihāra."
"If you had carried it back without knowing that, your head would have fallen off, even though I told you so—yes, I told you so! (ChU 1.11.9)
Now, therefore, follows the Udgītha of the dogs. Once, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to recite his sacred study.
For him, a white dog appeared.
Other dogs approached it and said,
"May the venerable one sing for us food."
"Or rather, it is hunger," he said. (ChU 1.12.2)
He said to them, "Come to me right here in the morning.
Then Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, as some say—waited there for him.
Just as those who are about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra here on earth move forward, holding hands and joined together, even so did they glide forward.
Having sat down together, they uttered the sound "hiṅ."
Oṃ 3 pibā 3 ma.
Oṃ 3. The god Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and Savitṛ have brought food here.
This world indeed is the syllable *hāuk*.
The letter *hā* is Vāyu;
the letter *atha* is the Moon;
the letter *iha* is the Self.
Fire is the syllable *ī*. ChUp 1.13.1.
Āditya is the syllable ū;
Nihava is the syllable e;
the Viśve Devāḥ are the syllable auho-ī.
Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*;
breath is the *svara*;
food is the *yā*.
Speech is Virāj.
The thirteenth is the undefined stobha, the moving syllable *huṃ*.

Speech yields its milk for him who knows the milking of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food— he who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Sāmans, yes, he who knows the secret doctrine.
The meditation on the entire Sāman is indeed auspicious.
For what is auspicious, they call "Sāman," and what is inauspicious, they call "Asāman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)
Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with *sāman*"; by this they mean, "He has approached him with what is good.
Or they say: "He has approached him without *sāman*"; by this they mean the opposite.
Then they also say: "It is *sāman* for us, alas! when something is good; they mean to say, "It is indeed good.
"It is not *sāman* for us, alas! when something is not good; they mean to say, "It is indeed not good."
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Sāman as "good"—verily, soon indeed may good dharmas come to him and attend upon him.
One should venerate the Sāman in five forms within the worlds:
the earth is the *hiṅkāra*,
and fire is the *prastāva*.
The intermediate space is the *udgītha*;
the sun is the *pratihāra*;
the sky is the *nidhana*.
Thus with regard to those who have ascended. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1)
Now, regarding the unobstructed [worlds]:
the sky is the *hiṅkāra*;
the sun is the *prastāva*.
The intermediate space is the Udgītha;
fire is the Pratihāra;
the earth is the Nidhana.
The worlds, both those above and those below, become favorable to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain:
the preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*;
the cloud that arises is the *prastāva*.
When it rains, that is the Udgītha;
when it flashes and thunders, that is the Pratihāra.
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain, seizes its finale and indeed causes it to rain. ChUp 2.3.2.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters:
when the cloud gathers, that is the *hiṅkāra*;
when it rains, that is the *prastāva*.
Those rivers that flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those that flow westward are the *pratihāra*;
the ocean is the *nidhana*.
He does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons:
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*,
Summer is the *prastāva*.
The rainy season is the *udgītha*;
autumn is the *pratihāra*;
winter is the *nidhana*.
The seasons serve him; he becomes possessed of the seasons, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals:
goats are the *hiṅkāra*,
sheep are the *prastāva*.
Cows are the Udgītha;
the horse is the Pratihāra;
the person is the Nidhana.
Cattle attend him and he becomes possessed of cattle, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in cattle.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman that is progressively higher among the vital breaths:

One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it.

For these are the parts that receive the first portion of this Sāman.

This Vāmadevya [Sāman] is woven into the couple.

He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;

Great in fame; he should not avoid anyone whatsoever—that is his vow. ChUp 2.13.2.
The rising sun is the *hiṅkāra*; the risen sun is the *prastāva*;

This Bṛhat Sāman is woven into the sun.

One should not find fault with it when it rains;

Spring is the *hiṅkāra*;

He who thus knows this Vairāja [Sāman] as interwoven within the seasons shines forth with offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge.

The earth is the *hiṅkāra*; the intermediate space is the *prastāva*;

The quarters are the Pratihāra;

These Śakvarī verses are woven upon the worlds.

and lives radiantly.

He should not revile the worlds.
That is the vow. ChUp 2.17.2.
The goats are the *hiṅkāra*;

The horses are the Pratihāra;

This Rājana chant is interwoven with the deities.

That is the vow, that is the vow.

That which is unexpressed belongs to Prajāpati;

Now, when the morning litany has been commenced, if the Brahman priest does not speak out before the concluding verse, they prepare both paths;
neither one is lost.

Agni from the earth.

from it, as it was being brooded upon, he drew out its essences:

By means of the very essence of the Sāmans, by the power of the Sāmans, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured on account of the Sāmans.
It is as follows: one might join gold with salt;

Indeed, that sacrifice is made medicinal where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus.

The human being is but a single priest; it is Brahman alone who protects the Kurus and the horses.

Breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best.

He who knows the foundation indeed stands firm in this world and in that world;
the eye, verily, is the foundation.
Verily, he who knows attainment—for him both divine and human desires attain fulfillment.
The ear, indeed, is attainment.
Verily, he who knows the abode becomes the abode of his own people;
for the mind, indeed, is the abode.
Then, indeed, the vital breaths (prāṇas) disputed among themselves as to who was superior, each saying, "I am superior!
I am superior!"
Those vital breaths (prāṇas) went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best?
He said to them, "He among you,
upon whose departure this body appears most wretched, he is the best of you."
Then Speech departed.
Having been away for a year, she returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as the limbs live without speaking, breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—so it was.
Then Speech entered [the body]. ChU 5.1.8.
The eye departed.

Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me? They replied:

It entered the ear. ChU 5.1.10.
The mind departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said:

Then the vital breath (*prāṇa*), about to depart, pulled out the other vital breaths just as a fine horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers;
they gathered around him and said,

Then Speech said to him:

Then Sight said to him:

Then the ear said to him:

Then the mind said to him:

Indeed, they do not call them "speeches," nor "eyes," nor "ears," nor "minds";

He indeed becomes a gainer of clothing;

Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas.

"Do you know where creatures go when they depart from here?
"No, venerable sir.

"No, Venerable Sir.
"Do you know where the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers—diverge?
"No, Venerable Sir. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.2)
"Do you know how that world is not filled?
"No, venerable sir.
"Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?"
"Certainly not, Blessed One," [he replied]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3)
Then [the father] said, "What have you been instructed? For how could one who does not know these things claim to have been instructed?
Distressed, he went to his father's side.

"A kinsman of royalty has asked me five questions, and I was not able to explain even one of them. He said, "Since you spoke to me in this way, it is as if I myself do not know even one of these."
"If I had known these, why would I not have told them to you? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.5)
Gautama went to the king's court. When he had arrived, the king offered him the honors due to him. He rose from his seat in the morning after having partaken of the hospitality.

He replied:

He said to him,

"So that this knowledge, which formerly did not go to the Brāhmaṇas from anyone before you, might [remain so]; therefore, indeed, in all the worlds, the governance belongs to the Kṣatriya alone. He said to him: "Speak! (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.7).
"Yonder world, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire.
Of that, the sun is the fuel;
the rays are the smoke."
The day is its flame;
the moon is its embers;
the stars are its sparks. (ChU 5.4.1)
In this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation;
from that oblation, King Soma comes into being.
Parjanya, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire;
its fuel is the wind,
and its smoke is the cloud.
The lightning is its flame; the thunderbolt is its embers;
and the thunderclaps are its sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma;
from that oblation, rain comes into being.
The earth, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Of that, the year is the fuel;
space is the smoke.
The night is its flame;
the quarters are its embers;
the intermediate quarters are its sparks.
Into this very fire the gods offer rain;
from that oblation food comes into being.
Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. His speech is the fuel;
his breath is the smoke.
The tongue is the flame;
the eyes are the embers;
the ears are the sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer food;
from that oblation, semen comes into being.
Woman, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Her lap is the fuel;
when he addresses her, that is the smoke.
The womb is the flame;
what he does within is the embers;
his pleasures are the sparks. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.8.1)
Into this very fire the gods offer semen;
from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
Thus, it is said that at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called "man.
Enveloped by the amnion, the embryo lies within for ten or nine months, or however long it may be, and then it is born.
Once born, he lives as long as his lifespan lasts.
When he has departed, they carry that deceased man from here back to the very fire from which he came and from which he was produced.
Now, those who know this thus,
and those who in the forest worship with faith, thinking "this is austerity"—
they pass into the light.
From the rays [of light] he goes to the day;
from the day to the waxing fortnight;
from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward. ChUp 5.10.1.
From the months [he goes] to the year;
from the year to the sun;
from the sun to the moon.
From the moon, to lightning;
there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman.
"This is the path of the gods. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.2)
Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, "Sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts," they pass into smoke;
from smoke, into night.

From the night [of the new moon] they go to the second half of the month; from the second half of the month, those six months during which the sun moves southward—these do not reach the year. ChU 5.10.3.
From the months, to the world of the fathers;
from the world of the fathers, to space;
from space, to the moon.
This is King Soma;
that is the food of the gods;
the gods consume it.
Having dwelt there for the duration of the twinkling of an eye, they then return again by this very same path:
to the ether; from the ether, to the air.
Having become air, he becomes smoke;
having become smoke, he becomes mist.

having become a cloud, it rains.
These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. From this state, indeed, it is most difficult to emerge.
For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, that very person comes into being again.
Therefore, those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, it is likely, attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya.
But those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is likely, attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla.
Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning creatures, subject to the cycle of "be born and die.
This is the third station.
Because of this, that world is not filled up.
Therefore, one should feel revulsion toward it.
On this point, there is this verse: Thus ends Chapter 5, Section 10, Verse 8 of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The thief of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor,

This indeed is the universal-formed Self, Vaiśvānara, whom you worship as the Self;
therefore, many things of manifold forms are seen in your family.

he eats food and sees what is dear.
He who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family a luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).

The first oblation he should offer, he should offer with the words, "Svāhā to Prāṇa!

when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied;
when the sun is satisfied, the sky is satisfied.

Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.

when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied;
when Agni is satisfied, the earth is satisfied.
When the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and fire together preside over is satisfied.

when the mind is satisfied, Parjanya is satisfied;
when Parjanya is satisfied, lightning is satisfied.

Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.

There was once Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi.
His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student.
For, my dear, no one in our family has ever been unlearned in the Vedas and yet remained like a mere Brahmin by birth."
Having approached [his teacher] at the age of twelve, he returned at twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he came home.
His father said to him: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2*
"Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so high-minded, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and so arrogant—

have you perhaps asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? How, indeed, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about?"

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4)

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold, everything made of gold would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.5)
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'iron' alone is the reality—
so, my dear, does that instruction become. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6)
"Surely those venerable ones did not know this;
for if they had known it, why would they not have told it to me?
Let the venerable one himself tell it to me."
"So be it," he said, "O Soma."
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning, this was Non-being alone, one only, without a second;
from that Non-being, Being was born. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
"But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? he said.
"How could being be born from non-being? Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone—one only, without a second."
It thought: "May I become many; may I procreate.
It emitted heat.
That heat (tejas) thought:
"May I become many; may I procreate.

Therefore, whenever a person grieves or perspires, from that very heat water is produced.
Of these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born.
That deity thought:
"Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2)
"Let me make each of these three deities threefold.
This very deity, having entered these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), differentiated names and forms.
Of these, he made each one threefold.
"Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three divinities becomes threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.4)
That which is the red form of Agni is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The fire-nature of fire has departed; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1)
That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;

The nature of the sun has departed from the sun;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone are the truth.
That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The moon-ness of the moon has departed;
modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of lightning is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The lightning-nature of lightning has departed;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone are the truth.
Knowing this, indeed, those of old—the great householders and great Vedic scholars—used to say:
"Nowadays, no one will be able to cite anything to us that has not been heard, not thought, or not understood.

"That which appeared as if red—that they recognized as the form of fire; that which appeared as if white—that they recognized as the form of water; and that which appeared as if black—that they recognized as the form of food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.6)

Or, as for that which seemed as if unknown, they understood it to be the combination of these very deities. "Now, my dear, learn from me how each one of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7)
Food that has been eaten is divided into three parts:
its grossest constituent becomes feces;
its middle constituent becomes flesh.
That which is the subtlest is the mind.
The water that is drunk is divided into three parts:
its grossest constituent becomes urine;
its middle constituent becomes blood.
That which is the subtlest is the vital breath (prāṇa).
The consumed fire is divided into three parts:
its coarsest constituent becomes bone,
and its middle constituent becomes marrow.
That which is the subtlest is speech.
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
the vital breath consists of water;
and speech consists of heat."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].

Of the fire, my dear, when it is being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;

"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
the vital breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."

Therefore they say of him,

"Just as a bird tied by a string, after flying in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon its very bond;

Pervaded by this living self, it stands drinking deeply and rejoicing."
When the life-force (jīva) leaves one branch of this tree, that branch withers;

"In this very way, my dear, understand it," he said.

That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self."
That is the Truth;
that is the Self;
"That thou art, Śvetaketu."

he is burned and then slain. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.1)
Now, if he is not the doer of that [crime],
then by that very truth he makes himself true.
Being committed to truth, having concealed himself with truth, he takes up the heated axe.
He is not burned;
then he is released.
Just as it would not be burned there,

This, Venerable Sir..."
I meditate upon him. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2)
Therefore, O Blessed One, I am indeed a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self.
For I have heard from those like your reverence that "the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
Thus, O Blessed One, I am in sorrow.
"May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow.
He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here is indeed nothing but Name."
Namely: the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas,

the Veda of the Vedas, the Pitrya, the Rashis, the Daiva, the Nidhi, the Vakovakya, the Ekayana, the Devavidya, the Brahmavidya, the Bhutavidya, the Kshatravidya, the Nakshatravidya, and the Sarpadevajanavidya.
"It is merely Name. Meditate upon Name. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.4)
He who meditates on "Name" as Brahman—
so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom, he who meditates on "Name" as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than Name?"
"Verily, there is something greater than name. May the Blessed One tell that to me."

Speech, indeed, is greater than name. Speech, indeed, makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, the science of the gods, and the science of spirits.

The knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of beings, the knowledge of the ruling power, the knowledge of the stars, the knowledge of serpents and divine beings; heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire; gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey, down to insects, moths, and ants; and both righteousness and unrighteousness.

Both truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant—if speech did not exist, neither dharma nor adharma would be made known, nor truth, nor falsehood, nor the good, nor the bad, nor the pleasant, nor the unpleasant. It is speech alone that makes all this known; therefore, venerate speech. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1)
He who venerates speech as Brahman—
so far as speech extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who venerates speech as Brahman.

All evils turn back from it.
For this world of Brahman is indeed free from evil.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even if he is blind, he becomes sighted; even if he is pierced, he becomes unpierced; even if he is afflicted by disease, he becomes free from affliction.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even though it is night, one arrives at day alone;
for this world of Brahman is indeed ever-shining.
Therefore, those who discover this world of Brahman through celibacy (brahmacarya)—for them alone is this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (yajña) is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya);
for by means of celibacy alone does one who knows find that [Brahman].
And that which they call "offering" (iṣṭa) is indeed celibacy.
For it is by means of the practice of celibacy that one, having performed sacrifice, finds the Self.

Now, that which they call the *sattrāyaṇa* sacrifice is simply celibacy (*brahmacarya*), for by means of celibacy one finds protection for oneself while existing. And that which they call "silence" (*mauna*) is simply celibacy.
For it is indeed by means of the holy life (brahmacarya) that one, having discovered the Self, reflects upon it.
Now, that which they call "the path of non-destruction" is indeed brahmacarya;
for this Self does not perish, which one finds through brahmacarya.
And that which they call "the path of the forest" is indeed brahmacarya.
Now, Ara and Nya, the two oceans, are in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here;
there is the lake Airammadīya,
and there is the Aśvattha tree called Somasavana.
That is the invincible city of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord.
Therefore, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)—to them alone belongs this world of Brahman;
for them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
Now, those channels of the heart—white, blue, yellow, and red—exist as subtle as a fine hair.
That sun is the one that is tawny; it is the white one, it is the blue one, it is the yellow one, and it is the red one.
Just as a great highway stretches out and goes to two villages—this one and that one—so too these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one.
They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels;
they extend from these channels and have entered into yonder sun.
When, being thus asleep, composed, and serene, one does not perceive any dream,
then he has entered into these channels;
no evil whatsoever touches him.
For at that time, he becomes endowed with splendor.
Then, when he has been reduced to weakness, those sitting around him say, "Do you recognize me? Do you recognize me?
as long as he has not yet departed from this body.
Only so much does he know. 8.6.4.
Then, when he departs from this body,
he ascends upwards by means of these very rays;
he passes away either saying "Om" or simply "Hā."
As quickly as one can direct the mind, so swiftly does it go to the sun.
This, indeed, is the gate to the world, the path for the wise, and the obstruction for the ignorant.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; one of them extends to the crown of the head.
Ascending by that, one goes to immortality; the others lead in all directions for departing, for departing. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6)

"That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," thus spoke Prajāpati.
Both the gods and the asuras became aware of this.
They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires.
Indra went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the asuras.
Agreeing with one another, they both went into the presence of Prajāpati with sacrificial fuel in their hands.
The two of them lived as religious students for thirty-two years.
Prajāpati said to them: "Desiring what have you dwelt here?"

They both said: "That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires—such is the word of the venerable ones they proclaim. Desiring that, we have come here. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3)
Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Then [Naciketas asked]: "Venerable sir, that which is perceived in the water and that which is in the mirror—which of these is it?"
"This very one, indeed, is perceived within all these ends," he said.
"Look at yourselves in a bowl of water; whatever you do not understand of yourselves, tell that to me.
The two of them looked into the bowl of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?"
They both said, "Venerable sir, we see this entire self of ours exactly as it is, even to the hair and the nails. ChU 8.8.1.
Prajāpati said to them both, "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a pan of water.
Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, they both looked into the pan of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?"
They both said, "Just as we two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-clothed, and groomed, even so these two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-clothed, and groomed.
He said, "This is the Self;
this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
With their hearts at peace, the two of them departed.

Having observed them, Prajāpati said: "They depart without having perceived the Self and without having realized it; whichever of these two—whether gods or asuras—shall have this as their secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they shall perish.
With his heart thus pacified, Virocana went to the asuras.
To them he declared this secret doctrine (upaniṣad): "The Self alone is to be magnified here; the Self is to be served.
By magnifying the Self alone here and by serving the Self, one attains both worlds—this one and the one beyond. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.8.4)
Therefore, even today, they say of one who does not give here, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an Asura!
For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Asuras:
they adorn the corpse of the deceased with alms, clothing, and ornaments.
For by this means, they think they will conquer that world.
Then Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this danger:

"Just as indeed this [Self] becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed."
"Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes; I see no object of enjoyment here," [he said]. (ChU 8.9.1)
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart along with Virocana, desiring what have you come back?"

He said: "Just as indeed, O Venerable Sir, this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed."
"Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes; I see no enjoyment in this," [he said]. (ChU 8.9.2)
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said.
"But I shall explain this very matter further to you.
Dwell for another thirty-two years."
He lived there for another thirty-two years;
then he said to him:
"That which moves about being honored in a dream—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
With his heart calmed, he departed.
But he, without even reaching the gods, perceived this danger:
"Even if this body becomes blind, he (the self) remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame. He is not defiled by its defect. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.10.1)
It is not slain by the slaying of this [body],
nor does it waste away by the wasting of this [body];
yet they do indeed slay it.
It is as if it were being covered;
it feels as if it has encountered something unpleasant;
it even weeps, thinking, "I see nothing here that can be enjoyed."
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"Maghavan, since you have gone forth with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?"
He said:
"Venerable sir, even if this body becomes blind, he [the self] remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame.
Indeed, he is not affected by its defect."
It is not slain by the slaying of this [body], nor is it wounded by its wounding;
yet, as it were, they do slay it.
He feels as if being covered;
he feels as if experiencing something unpleasant;
he even feels as if weeping.
"I see no enjoyment here," [he said].
"It is just so, O Maghavan," he replied.
"I shall explain this very same thing to you further."
"Stay for another thirty-two years.
He lived there for another thirty-two years.
Then he said to him:
"Therefore, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.
With his heart at peace, he departed.
Having failed to reach the gods, he perceived this fear:
"Truly, this one does not now know himself as 'this is I,' nor indeed these beings."
"He has gone to utter destruction;
I see no enjoyment for him in this," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.1)
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?
He replied: "Indeed, venerable sir, one does not even now know oneself thus: 'This is I.'"
"In this way, these beings do not exist;
they have simply gone to destruction.
I see nothing here that can be enjoyed. Thus he spoke. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.2)
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said.
"I shall explain this very matter to you further; indeed, there is nothing other than this."
"Let me dwell for another five years.
He dwelt for another five years;
thus they amounted to one hundred and one.
This is what they say:
"For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati;
to him, [Prajāpati] said: ChUp 8.11.3.
O Maghavan, this mortal body is indeed seized by death;
it is the substrate for this immortal, bodiless self.
For that which possesses a body is indeed seized by pleasure and pain.
"For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant;
but for one who is truly bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1)
The wind is bodiless;
the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodiless.
Just as these, having risen from that sky and having reached the highest light, appear in their own true form.
In the very same way, this serene being, having arisen from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form.
He is the Supreme Person.
There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or with carriages, or with kinsmen, not remembering this body as a place of rebirth.
Just as a draft animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (prāṇa) yoked to this body.
Now, where this eye is directed toward space, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing.
Now, he who knows "let me smell this" is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. Now, he who knows "let me speak this" is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking.
Now, he who knows, "May I hear this," that is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing.
Now, he who knows "I am thinking this" is the Self;
the mind is his divine eye.
With that divine eye, the mind, he beholds these desires and rejoices in them which are in the world of Brahman.
The gods indeed worship this very Self;
therefore, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them.
He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires.
Thus indeed spoke Prajāpati; Prajāpati spoke.
From the dark I pass to the variegated; from the variegated I pass to the dark.

Like a horse shaking off its hairs, having shaken off evil, and like the moon freeing itself from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I—being one whose self is perfected—attain the uncreated world of Brahman; yes, I attain it.
Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form;
that which is between them is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self.
I enter the assembly hall and the abode of Prajāpati; may I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, the glory of the kings, the glory of the commoners.
"I have attained glory;
I am indeed the glory of glories.
O white, toothless one, toothless white one, do not come near me! Do not come near me! (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1)
Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his progeny.

Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the prescribed rule, and having returned home with the remainder of the time after performing service for the teacher, he should settle in a household, reciting his private Vedic study in a clean place, maintaining righteous conduct, withdrawing all his senses into himself, and practicing non-violence.
Except for the sacrificial fires, [he offers] all beings as oblations.
Indeed, conducting himself thus throughout his life, he reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again, does not return again.
